content.text: In 1831, Michael Faraday made a discovery that would change the world: moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces an electric current. This phenomenon—electromagnetic induction—is the principle behind generators, transformers, and wireless charging. It's how most of the world's electricity is produced.

Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating a voltage by changing the magnetic flux through a conductor. A voltage is induced only when the flux is changing -- a stationary magnet near a coil produces no voltage.

content.text: Comparing Left and Right Hand Rules

Do not confuse Fleming's left-hand rule (motors) with the right-hand rule (generators). Left hand = motor effect (force on a wire). Right hand = generator effect (induced current). A common exam error is using the wrong hand.

"You need a complete circuit for induction"
— A voltage is induced whether or not there's a complete circuit. Current flows only if the circuit is complete.

Lenz's Law is a consequence of conservation of energy. The induced current always opposes the change that caused it. If you push a north pole into a coil, the coil becomes a north pole on that end to repel it -- you must do work against this opposition, and that work becomes the electrical energy.

Move a magnet into (or out of) the coil; move the coil relative to a magnet. Also valid: change the magnetic field strength through the coil, or rotate the coil in a field.
— There is no change in magnetic flux through the coil. Electromagnetic induction requires a changing flux, not merely the presence of a field. (explanation)
Move the magnet faster (greater rate of flux change), use a stronger magnet (greater flux density), increase the number of turns on the coil.
— Each increases the rate of change of flux linkage. (description)
Lenz's law states that the induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change causing it.
— If the induced current aided the change, the magnet would accelerate without any energy input, violating conservation of energy. Work must be done against the opposing force. (explanation)
The near end acts as a north pole.

— The south pole moving away means decreasing south-pointing flux. To oppose this decrease, the coil creates a south-pointing field towards the magnet, which means the far end is south and the near end (facing the retreating magnet) is north. The north pole attracts the departing south pole, opposing the motion. (application)
EMF = n x (change in flux / time) = 50 x (0.01 / 0.05) = 50 x 0.2 = 10 V

When braking, the electric motor acts as a generator. The wheels drive the motor coil in the magnetic field, inducing a voltage that drives current back into the battery. By Lenz's law, the induced current creates a force opposing the motion, slowing the vehicle. Kinetic energy is converted to electrical energy stored in the battery rather than wasted as heat.
